name: COLE, J.
description: Concurred, finding Judge Medley violated judicial conduct rules by making knowingly false campaign statements and failing to report expenditures, justifying a 30-day suspension.

name: WEIMER, C.J.
description: Concurred, arguing that while political speech, especially in judicial campaigns, deserves heightened First Amendment protection, knowingly false statements are not protected and the delay in proceedings was excessive.

name: Griffin, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the plain text of the Louisiana Constitution and decades of jurisprudence prohibit joining capital and non-capital felony charges.

name: Hughes, J.
description: Concurred, argued that capital cases have a different jury selection process and the jury determines the penalty, making the mode of trial different.

name: Crain, J.
description: Concurred with Justice Cole's reasoning.

name: McCallum, J.
description: Dissented, argued that joinder is constitutionally permissible due to judicial economy and because all charges are absolute felonies from the same incident, and the "mode of trial" distinction is no longer relevant after Ramos.

name: Cole, J.
description: Concurred in the result, argued that statutory provisions prohibit joinder, making the majority's constitutional analysis unnecessary.

name: CRAIN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Act 437 is unconstitutional because historical horse racing is a new form of gaming not authorized before October 15, 1996, and thus requires prior voter approval by local election.

name: CRAIN, J
description: Concurred, argued that the statute is constitutional as it is rationally related to the legitimate government interest of ensuring access to healthcare during a public health emergency, and does not violate due process or the prohibition against special laws.

name: GRIFFIN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the statute's plain language leads to absurd consequences when applied to injuries unrelated to the public health emergency, and therefore the plaintiff should not be required to plead gross negligence.

name: KNOLL, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the court should avoid constitutional questions if the case could be resolved on nonconstitutional grounds, and believed the statute should not apply as the plaintiff's injuries were not related to the public health emergency.

name: Hughes, J.
description: Concurred, argued that La. R.S. 13:4163 is unconstitutional because it usurps the judiciary's power to manage its docket and violates the separation of powers doctrine.

name: Weimer, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the statute is unconstitutional on its face because its mandatory, ex parte aspects remove judicial discretion, intruding on the judiciary's inherent powers to administer courts and ensure fair justice.

name: McCallum, J.
description: Dissented, argued that while the statute can be abused, the majority's broad ruling is too destructive and a narrower remedy should have been applied, and that the issue was nearly moot.

name: Weimer, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the defendant failed to meet his burden of proving prejudice from counsel's performance.

name: Crichton, J.
description: Concurred, emphasized the importance of the right to effective assistance of counsel at sentencing and that the defendant was entitled to a new sentencing hearing.

name: Crain, J.
description: Dissented, argued that even if counsel's performance was deficient, it did not prejudice the defendant, as the sentence was not excessive enough to warrant a downward departure.

name: McCallum, J.
description: Dissented with majority opinion.

name: GENOVESE, J.
description: Concurred, affirming the appellate court's decision that mandamus is appropriate for enforcing inverse condemnation judgments.

name: WEIMER, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the constitutional obligation to pay compensation for property taken is tempered by the need to demonstrate conscious indifference to payment for mandamus to be appropriate.

name: GRIFFIN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that self-executing and mandatory provisions of the Declaration of Rights, like the one protecting against inverse condemnation, are distinguishable from contract and tort claims for enforcement.

name: Weimer, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the legislature has the authority to retroactively revive prescribed claims for child sexual abuse, as the defendants' right to claim liberative prescription is not an absolute vested property right and the revival provisions pass the rational basis test under due process.

name: Hughes, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority opinion sets a bad precedent by elevating legislative acts over constitutional rights and obliterating the vested right of accrued prescription, and that the decision grants unbridled authority to the legislature.

name: Crichton, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the majority correctly overruled Burmaster and that vested rights are subject to due process analysis, finding the legislation rationally related to a compelling government interest.

name: Genovese, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority opinion elevates legislative acts over constitutional rights, obliterates the vested right of accrued prescription, and grants unbridled authority to the legislature, setting a bad precedent.

name: Griffin, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the right to assert prescription is not a fundamental right and the legislation is rationally related to a legitimate government interest, allowing victims their day in court.

name: GENOVESE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the statutory enactment reviving prescribed child sex abuse claims is unconstitutional as it violates due process protections by disturbing defendants' vested property rights in accrued prescription.

name: WEIMER, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the legislature has the authority to revive prescribed claims for child sexual abuse, and the majority incorrectly elevates a procedural right (accrued prescription) above fundamental rights and misapplies due process analysis.

name: CRICHTON, J.
description: Concurred, agreed with the majority's conclusion that the revival provisions are unconstitutional but emphasized the importance of the remedy of 'contra non valentem' which may still be available to the victims.

name: GRIFFIN, J.
description: Concurred, generally agreed with the majority's legal principles but emphasized the necessity to adhere to constitutional tenets and ensure fundamental fairness, acknowledging the horrific nature of the allegations.

name: McCALLUM, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court's order to remit funds into its registry violated constitutional provisions regarding public funds and legislative appropriation, thus overstepping judicial authority and infringing on the separation of powers.

name: WEIMER, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the underlying ordinance was constitutional, making the collected fines properly acquired, and questioned the court's use of plenary authority to review an untimely challenged judgment.

name: Hughes, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the case is about returning unconstitutionally taken property, not enforcing a money judgment against a governmental entity.

name: CRICHTON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Article 930.10 unconstitutionally allows the judicial branch to exercise the governor's exclusive pardon power, violating the separation of powers.

name: WEIMER, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the attorney general's writ application should be dismissed due to procedural issues (standing and timeliness) and that Article 930.10 is constitutional as a post-conviction process, not a pardon.

name: GRIFFIN J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Louisiana Constitution framers intended the legislature to have an expansive pardon power supplementary to the governor's, making Article 930.10 constitutional.

name: Retired Judge Paul Bonin
description: Dissented with majority opinion.

name: McCALLUM, J.
description: Concurred, argued that absolute prosecutorial immunity applies to prosecutors for actions within the judicial phase of the criminal process, even for intentional misconduct, and that statutory exceptions do not override this doctrine.

name: WEIMER, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that plaintiffs are not afforded a legal remedy for damages against the ADA and DA, and that Louisiana law should prioritize statutory enactments over judicial decisions for immunity.

name: Hughes, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the assistant district attorney's intentional dishonest acts were outside the scope of his duties, and therefore, he should not be immune from a cause of action.

name: GRIFFIN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the abatement ab initio doctrine is obsolete and inconsistent with positive law, and should be abandoned to ensure convictions stand and victims' rights are considered.

name: Crichton, J.
description: Dissented in part, argued that while the doctrine is obsolete, the trial court's notation should explicitly state 'Appeal Dismissed; Conviction Final' to ensure the finality of the conviction, especially given the heinous nature of the crimes.

name: SJC
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: JLW
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: JTG
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: JBM
description: Concurred with majority opinion.

name: PDG Hughes, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while counsel may have failed to apprise the court of its duty, the duty to ensure a just sentence ultimately rests with the court.

name: Crain, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the court is jurisprudentially expanding post-conviction review beyond legislative authority and potentially stripping trial courts of their constitutional role in sentencing.

name: CRICHTON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Ramos jury unanimity rule does not apply retroactively to cases on state collateral review due to reliance interests, administrative burden, and the state's prospective constitutional amendment.

name: Weimer, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Ramos rule is not a Teague "watershed rule" and its retroactive application is outweighed by finality and reliance interests.

name: Genovese, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that Ramos is not broadly retroactive but relief should be granted for non-unanimous verdicts tainted by racial animus upon proof.

name: McCallum, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Ramos is not retroactive on collateral review, emphasizing the importance of finality in criminal judgments.

name: Griffin, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Ramos should apply retroactively as a watershed rule addressing a racially discriminatory system and ensuring fundamental fairness.

name: MCCALLUM, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the LCB exceeded its delegated authority by creating a new restriction on trust fund income that was not contemplated by the legislature, thereby acting in a legislative capacity in violation of the separation of powers doctrine.

name: MCCALLUM, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the SBSEP is unconstitutional because it violates Louisiana Constitution Article VI, Section 5(G) and Article VIII, Section 10(A) by forcing the School Board, an independent state entity, to administer the program, thereby exceeding the parish's legislative authority.

name: WEIMER, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the SBSEP is constitutional because it aids the School Board in protecting school children, does not impermissibly mandate the School Board, and is not inconsistent with the constitution or law, as the constitutional prohibition applies to charters, not ordinances.

name: CRICHTON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Act 3 created a new tax by making previously untaxed transactions taxable, and its failure to secure a supermajority vote rendered it unconstitutional under the Tax Limitation Clause.

name: Weimer, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that Act 3 merely clarified the prior law regarding the further processing exclusion and did not create a new tax, thus not requiring a two-thirds vote.

name: Hughes, J.
description: Dissented, for the reasons assigned by Weimer, C.J.

name: GENOVESE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the award of attorney fees and litigation costs to defendants is upheld based on the Louisiana Constitution of 1974, not statutory law.

name: Weimer, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Louisiana Constitution of 1974 provides a basis for upholding the award of attorney fees and litigation costs, highlighting the history of Article I, § 4.

name: Crain, J.
description: Dissented in part, argued that an award of attorney fees is not appropriate when the property owner recovers an amount equal to or less than the pre-suit offer, as such fees were not caused by the expropriation.

name: McCallum, J.
description: Concurred with the reasons assigned by Weimer, C.J.

name: GRIFFIN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the municipality has a ministerial duty to appropriate funds for statutorily and constitutionally mandated back wages owed to firefighters, making a writ of mandamus an appropriate remedy.

name: Retired Judge Robert L. Lobrano
description: Concurred with majority opinion

name: Hughes, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the matter involves enforcing a money judgment against a public body, which is a political decision, not a judicial one, and constitutional/statutory protections against such enforcement should not be discarded.
